**Enigma Variations**
Elgar's 1899 orchestral work, formally titled Variations on an Original Theme, dedicated "to my friends pictured within." Each of its fourteen variations is a musical portrait of a friend or family member, labeled with initials or nicknames. The "enigma" refers to a hidden larger theme that supposedly "goes" with the main theme but is never played, and whose identity Elgar never revealed.

**"Nimrod"**
The ninth and most famous of the Enigma Variations, a slow, noble movement portraying Elgar's friend and editor at the publisher Novello, Augustus J. Jaeger. "Nimrod" is a pun: Jäger means "hunter" in German, and Nimrod is the "mighty hunter" of the Bible. The variation was inspired by a conversation about the slow movements of Beethoven, and it echoes the Adagio of Beethoven's Pathétique Sonata.

**Pomp and Circumstance Marches**
A set of military marches for orchestra (five completed in his lifetime, a sixth assembled posthumously from sketches). The first, in D major, is played at nearly every American high school and college graduation ceremony.

**"Land of Hope and Glory"**
The broad trio melody from Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, which Elgar reused in his Coronation Ode for King Edward VII (1902) with words by A. C. Benson. It became a patriotic British anthem, sung every year at the Last Night of the Proms.

**The Dream of Gerontius**
Elgar's 1900 oratorio setting a poem by Cardinal John Henry Newman. It follows the dying Gerontius, called "the Soul" after his death, as he is guided by his Guardian Angel to judgment before God; a huge orchestral climax depicts his momentary glimpse of God, and he is then sent to Purgatory. Famous passages include Gerontius's "Sanctus fortis," the Priest's "Go forth upon thy journey, Christian soul," the chorus "Praise to the Holiest in the height," and the plea of the Angel of the Agony.

**Cello Concerto in E minor**
Elgar's last major work (1919), written in the aftermath of World War I. It opens with a dramatic solo cello recitative, after which the violas introduce a flowing theme in 9/8. Its 1919 premiere with soloist Felix Salmond was a disaster because of insufficient rehearsal time, but Jacqueline du Pré's 1965 recording with John Barbirolli made it one of the most popular cello concertos.

**"Dorabella"**
Variation X of the Enigma Variations, an intermezzo portraying Dora Penny, a young friend of the Elgars. Light, fluttering woodwind thirty-second notes gently imitate her slight stutter or her laugh.

**"C.A.E."**
The first variation of the Enigma Variations, a tender portrait of Elgar's wife, Caroline Alice Elgar. Other variations include "R.P.A." (Richard Penrose Arnold), "Ysobel" (Isabel Fitton, a viola student), and the finale "E.D.U." (a self-portrait based on Alice's pet name for him, "Edu").

**Salut d'Amour**
A short salon piece for violin and piano (originally titled Liebesgruss), which Elgar wrote in 1888 as an engagement present for Caroline Alice Roberts, who became his wife. It became one of his most popular small works.

**Introduction and Allegro**
A 1905 work for string quartet and string orchestra that imitates the Baroque concerto grosso and includes a fugal section. Its "Welsh" theme, first heard on solo viola, was inspired by the distant sound of singing Elgar heard on a cliff in Wales. It shares its title with an Introduction and Allegro by Maurice Ravel composed the same year.

**Violin Concerto in B minor**
Elgar's 1910 violin concerto, which contains several "Windflower" themes named after his nickname for his friend Alice Stuart-Wortley. The score bears the mysterious Spanish inscription "Aquí está encerrada el alma de ....." ("Herein is enshrined the soul of .....").

**Symphony No. 1 in A-flat major**
Elgar's 1908 first symphony, which opens with a broad, stately motto theme marked "nobilmente" in A-flat major. It was premiered and championed by the conductor Hans Richter, who also led the premiere of the Enigma Variations.

**Symphony No. 2 in E-flat major**
Elgar's 1911 second symphony, dedicated to the memory of King Edward VII and described by Elgar as "the passionate pilgrimage of a soul." It is headed by a quotation from Shelley, "Rarely, rarely, comest thou, Spirit of Delight." His sketches for a Third Symphony were completed by Anthony Payne in 1997.

**"Romanza"**
The thirteenth and penultimate variation of the Enigma Variations, labeled only with three asterisks. A clarinet quotes a phrase from Mendelssohn's overture Calm Sea and Prosperous Voyage over a soft timpani roll (often played with coins or hard sticks) that imitates the throb of a ship's engines, possibly referring to a friend on a sea voyage.

**Concert overtures and Sea Pictures**
Elgar wrote programmatic orchestral pieces such as the Froissart overture, Cockaigne (In London Town), which depicts London, In the South (Alassio), and the "symphonic study" Falstaff in C minor. His orchestral song cycle Sea Pictures for contralto includes "Where Corals Lie" and "The Swimmer."
